description: Profumo, legalising homosexuality, CND, and the student protests that challenged deference in the 1960s.
content_html:
The Permissive Society

The 1960s are often labelled the era of the permissive society — a time when laws, attitudes, and social norms shifted away from the conformity of the 1950s towards greater individual freedom. Within a decade, Britain decriminalised homosexuality, abolished the death penalty, relaxed divorce law, legalised abortion, and ended theatre censorship. All these reforms happened under Home Secretary Roy Jenkins between 1965 and 1967, a period sometimes called the “permissive moment.”

Whether these changes were truly “permissive” — a morally neutral extension of liberty — or represented a breakdown of moral standards, was fiercely debated at the time and has been argued over ever since. Critics such as Mary Whitehouse, who founded the National Viewers’ and Listeners’ Association in 1965, argued that television and the new laws were corroding public morality. Supporters argued that the reforms simply brought the law into line with how many people already lived.

Key Fact

The Profumo Affair of 1963 was one of the most damaging political scandals of the post-war era. John Profumo, Harold Macmillan’s Secretary of State for War, had an affair with Christine Keeler, who was simultaneously involved with Yevgeny Ivanov, a Soviet naval attaché. Profumo denied the affair in a personal statement to the House of Commons, then admitted he had lied. He resigned in June 1963. The scandal contributed significantly to Macmillan’s own resignation later that year and to the Conservatives’ defeat in 1964.

The Legalisation of Homosexuality

Before 1967, sexual acts between men were criminal offences in England and Wales, carrying penalties of up to life imprisonment. The law was applied inconsistently but had ruined many lives — the 1952 prosecution and chemical castration of mathematician Alan Turing being one of the most notorious examples. The Sexual Offences Act 1967 decriminalised private consensual acts between men aged 21 or over in England and Wales (Scotland and Northern Ireland followed much later).

The Act was a partial liberalisation. The age of consent remained 21 (higher than the heterosexual age of 16), and it did not apply to the armed forces or the merchant navy. Public attitudes towards homosexuality remained largely hostile, and discrimination in employment and housing was widespread. Nevertheless, the Act was a significant legal milestone that began a process of reform that would continue for decades.

Capital punishment for murder was suspended by the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 and abolished permanently in 1969 (though it remained for treason and certain other offences until 1998). The campaign to abolish hanging had been strengthened by several controversial executions: the hanging of Derek Bentley in 1953 despite doubts about his responsibility, and the execution of Timothy Evans in 1950 (later exonerated after it emerged that the serial killer John Christie had committed the murders Evans was convicted of).

The miscarriage of justice in the Evans case and concerns about executing the innocent made the arguments for abolition more persuasive. Ruth Ellis, hanged in 1955 and the last woman executed in Britain, also attracted public sympathy. Opinion polls at the time suggested a majority opposed abolition, making this a case where Parliament acted against popular opinion on a matter of principle.

CND and Nuclear Protest

The CND — the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament — was founded in 1958 in response to British nuclear weapons testing and the growing fear of nuclear war. Its annual marches from the Atomic Weapons Establishment at Aldermaston in Berkshire to London drew tens of thousands of participants. CND attracted support from across the political spectrum, including scientists, clergy, intellectuals, and young people.

CND’s membership peaked in the early 1960s during the Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962), when the world came closest to nuclear war. The peace symbol (designed by Gerald Holtom in 1958 specifically for CND) became one of the most recognisable political symbols of the twentieth century. CND was associated with a broader critique of Cold War politics, American foreign policy, and Britain’s junior role in the Western alliance. The movement waned after the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty, though it revived in the 1980s in response to Cruise missile deployment.

Key Fact

CND’s first Aldermaston march took place at Easter 1958; it attracted an estimated 4,000 marchers from London to Aldermaston. From 1959 onwards the march ran from Aldermaston to London and drew tens of thousands of participants. It was one of the largest peace movements in British history.

Student Protest, 1968

1968 was a year of global protest. In France, student uprisings brought the country close to revolution. In the United States, anti-Vietnam War protests convulsed campuses. In Britain, the most dramatic moment came on 17 March 1968, when approximately 10,000 people marched to the American Embassy in Grosvenor Square in London to protest against the Vietnam War. Several hundred demonstrators attempted to rush the embassy; there were 246 arrests and more than 50 injured.

Student activism spread through British universities. Sit-ins, occupations, and demands for student representation on university governing bodies became common. Students at the London School of Economics were particularly active. The protests reflected a generation questioning not only foreign policy but also the structures of educational authority, class deference, and what they saw as the hypocrisy of the political establishment. The Profumo Affair had already shown that the ruling class was not morally superior; 1968 challenged whether it was politically legitimate.

Drug use, particularly cannabis and LSD, became associated with youth culture and the counter-culture of the 1960s. The Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 created the classification system (Class A, B, C) still in use today, and significantly increased penalties for supply. High-profile prosecutions, including the 1967 arrests of Rolling Stones members Mick Jagger and Keith Richards for drug possession, became part of the cultural conflict between establishment authority and youth culture. The Times published a full-page advertisement calling for cannabis law reform, signed by 65 prominent people including Beatles member Paul McCartney.

The tension between the permissive liberalisation in some areas of law and increasing restrictions in others (such as drugs) illustrated the contradictory nature of the “permissive society.” Roy Jenkins’s reforms aimed to expand personal liberty in private behaviour; drug law remained firmly restrictive on public safety grounds.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the permissive society, avoid the temptation to list all the reforms without explaining their significance. For ‘8 marks — Explain Significance’, argue: what did these changes mean at the time (lived impact on people’s lives) and what did they mean over time (did they represent a permanent shift in attitudes or law)? For ‘10 marks — Compare Interpretations’ questions about this period, focus on WHY historians disagree — not just what each interpretation says. A Thatcherite historian might see the 1960s as causing moral decline; a social historian might see it as overdue liberalisation. The key distinction is WHY (author’s standpoint, evidence used, era of writing) rather than just WHAT each says.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1960s saw significant liberalising legislation in England and Wales: homosexuality partly decriminalised (1967), the death penalty suspended (1965, abolished 1969), abortion legalised (1967), and divorce law reformed (1969).
  • The Profumo Affair (1963) damaged the Conservative government and eroded deference towards the political establishment; student protests of 1968 — especially the Grosvenor Square demonstration — reflected a generation willing to challenge authority directly.
  • CND (founded 1958) was one of the largest peace movements in British history, drawing tens of thousands to Aldermaston marches and reflecting broad public anxiety about nuclear weapons during the Cold War.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Profumo Affair of 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- John Profumo, Secretary of State for War, lied to Parliament about his affair with Christine Keeler; on admission, he resigned in June 1963.
- The affair raised national security concerns because Keeler was also linked to Yevgeny Ivanov, a Soviet naval attaché; the scandal contributed to Macmillan's resignation and the Conservatives' 1964 election defeat.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of CND (Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament) in the late 1950s and early 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include:
- Growing public fear of nuclear war after British nuclear tests and the escalation of the Cold War arms race; the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the world to the brink of nuclear war, swelling CND membership.
- Moral argument from scientists and clergy that nuclear weapons threatened mass civilian casualties and were ethically unacceptable.
- Opposition to Britain's dependence on American nuclear strategy and support for a specifically British 'third way' through unilateral disarmament.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Sexual Offences Act 1967.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- Private consensual acts between men aged 21 or over were no longer criminal; gay men could live without the immediate threat of prosecution, though discrimination in employment and public life continued.
- The Act was a partial reform with significant limitations (age 21 not 16; excluded armed forces); campaigners argued for full equality, which took decades to achieve.
- The 1967 Act began a legislative process that eventually produced equal age of consent (2001) and same-sex marriage (2014).

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant were the student protests of 1968 in challenging authority in Britain? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument.

At the time: 10,000 marched to Grosvenor Square; 246 arrested; university sit-ins spread; pressure for student representation in governance.
Over time: limited long-term impact on UK political structures compared to France; but part of a broader generational shift away from deference that shaped 1970s political culture.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The social reforms of the 1960s made Britain a more tolerant and fair society.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: Sexual Offences Act (1967) freed gay men from criminal prosecution; abolition of death penalty ended risk of executing the innocent; abortion Act saved women's lives; divorce reform freed people from unhappy marriages.

Disagreement: reforms were limited in scope (e.g. homosexuality for men aged 21+ only, not in armed forces); public attitudes remained hostile in many areas; women still faced discrimination; racial discrimination remained widespread (see immigration lesson); 'tolerance' was not equally available to all groups.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of CND's campaign methods in the late 1950s and early 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Annual marches between Aldermaston (Atomic Weapons Establishment) and London drew tens of thousands; the first march in Easter 1958 attracted an estimated 4,000 participants.
- CND used the peace symbol (designed by Gerald Holtom in 1958) as a highly visible and internationally recognised symbol of the nuclear disarmament cause.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

knowledge_checks.q: What did the Sexual Offences Act 1967 do?
options: Legalised homosexuality for all men over 18
Decriminalised private consensual acts between men aged 21 or over in England and Wales
Gave gay men the same legal rights as heterosexual people
Applied equally to Scotland and Northern Ireland

knowledge_checks.q: What was the Profumo Affair of 1963?
options: A scandal involving Harold Wilson's financial dealings
The discovery of nuclear weapons secrets being passed to China
War Minister John Profumo lying to Parliament about an affair with links to a Soviet attaché
A spy scandal involving a senior civil servant at GCHQ

flashcard_questions.a: 1963 — War Minister Profumo lied to Parliament about an affair; Keeler was also linked to a Soviet naval attaché.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Sexual Offences Act 1967 decriminalise?
flashcard_questions.a: Private consensual acts between men aged 21 or over in England and Wales.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) founded?
Where did CND's annual marches go to and from?
flashcard_questions.a: Between Aldermaston (Atomic Weapons Establishment) and London.

flashcard_questions.q: When was capital punishment for murder suspended in Britain?
What was the significance of the Grosvenor Square protest in March 1968?
flashcard_questions.a: Around 10,000 people marched against the Vietnam War; 246 were arrested — the most violent British protest of the 1960s.

flashcard_questions.q: Who founded the National Viewers' and Listeners' Association in 1965, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Mary Whitehouse — to campaign against what she saw as declining moral standards in broadcasting.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Roy Jenkins' reforms of 1965–1967 include?
flashcard_questions.a: Suspension of death penalty, homosexuality decriminalised, abortion legalised, divorce law reformed, theatre censorship ended.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 create?
flashcard_questions.a: A classification system (Class A, B, C) for illegal drugs, still in use today.

flashcard_questions.q: What scandal involving Ruth Ellis strengthened the case for abolishing the death penalty?
flashcard_questions.a: Ellis was the last woman hanged in Britain (1955); her case attracted public sympathy and fuelled abolitionist arguments.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the Timothy Evans case strengthen the abolition of capital punishment campaign?
flashcard_questions.a: Evans was hanged (1950) but later exonerated; John Christie had committed the murders, showing the risk of executing the innocent.

flashcard_questions.q: What did CND's Aldermaston marches protest against?
flashcard_questions.a: British nuclear weapons and demand for unilateral nuclear disarmament.

glossary_terms.definition: A social shift in the 1960s in which laws and attitudes became more tolerant of previously forbidden behaviours, including homosexuality, abortion, divorce, and drug use.

A 1963 political scandal in which War Minister John Profumo was found to have lied to Parliament about his affair with Christine Keeler, who was also linked to a Soviet military attaché, raising national security concerns.
An Act of Parliament (1967) that decriminalised private consensual sexual acts between men aged 21 or over in England and Wales.
The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, founded in 1958, which argued for unilateral British nuclear disarmament; associated with the Aldermaston marches.
Grosvenor Square in London, site of the American Embassy, where anti-Vietnam War protesters clashed with police in March 1968 in the most violent British demonstration of the decade.
The Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, which classified illegal drugs into Classes A, B, and C according to their perceived harmfulness.
